cells.tense: You are keeping it level here, with your hands on it right now.
cells.ask: Think of one person you are currently out of step with, and say out loud to yourself what a fair settling would look like — what you would give, what you would ask — then leave it there.
cells.core:
You can feel when something between you and another person has gone off true — a little more given than received, or the reverse — and you adjust before it turns into a problem. Most days that read of proportion runs on its own, and you trust it without working it out on paper. When the stakes are small, fairness costs you almost nothing, and the people around you can feel how even you keep things.

The loose place is ahead, not behind. When the correction costs you something real, you hold still a beat and let the other one move first. There is a person this would be about, and a thing you have not yet said. Working out what a fair settling would look like gets you ready to say it. Nothing more is asked of you tonight.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel when a thing between people has gone off true.
cells.place: the shared middle, where two people stand even

cells.tense: You will have already lost the ground you are trying to protect by evening the score.
cells.ask: Let one debt sit for a week. Write it down if the writing helps, then leave it until the week is up and do not raise it with anyone in between.
cells.core:
You are already at the end of a score you have not finished tallying. Someone says a sentence, and the exchange runs in you — what it costs, what it earns back, how it squares with the last three things. Most of that happens before you have decided to do it.

What it buys is protection from a bad turn that has not happened. What it costs is the person in front of you, who gets answered as a total rather than a remark. The accounting has a use when something really is out of balance. It stops being useful when it is running on transactions that are still going. Next time the account opens in you, try letting it stay open an hour. Not forgiving it. Just not settling it that same minute.

cells.tense: You have been standing in front of a door that closed a long time ago.
cells.ask: Once this week, when something is asked and the answer is no, say no plainly — one sentence — and let it stand with no explanation attached.
cells.core:
You take the smaller half and call yourself easygoing. When someone shortchanges you, some part of you finds a way to decide it is fine, and the finding-a-way is quick and practiced. So the plain sense of what belongs to you has gone quiet. Not generosity. Just the ordinary read of what is yours and what is not.

When it runs well, this looks small. You notice a thing is uneven, you say something out loud, and that is enough; nobody has to agree with you for the sentence to count. It will not come back by trying harder at the hard moment. It comes back practiced somewhere nothing rests on the answer — one clean no, one clean yes, in a place where it costs you little.
cells.sheetLine: You have stopped asking for your half.

cells.tense: You are keeping a tally right now that you would deny keeping if someone asked.
cells.ask: Catch one moment today when you quietly adjust for a favor given or skipped, and say out loud to yourself, in a plain sentence, what you just did.
cells.core:
There is a running count in you of small slights and skipped turns. You mention it to no one, and if someone named it you would say you keep no score at all. But the accounting is steering things anyway — in the small pause before you answer someone you feel you owe, or are owed.

When fairness is running clean, you spot what is out of balance and call it out loud, and the calling-out settles it. The count underneath is the same motion with the lights off. The moment you name it, the thing has already done the work it was doing. That is most of what is needed here: not a reckoning, just admitting there is one, in your own words, with the numbers still running.
